transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, hi. Um… honestly, work kind of pushed me to come in. I keep forgetting things I’m supposed to follow up on — like scheduled callbacks, work orders, little things I told people I’d take care of — and then they turn into big things because I just… don’t get back to them.

And it’s piled up. I do maintenance work, so there’s always something, someone needs a repair or a call back, and I’ll think, “Okay, I’ve got that,” and then somehow it’s gone. It’s embarrassing. They basically said I need to get this looked at before it costs me my chance to move up. Which I really need, because, you know, I’ve been trying to show I can handle more responsibility, and then I’m over here forgetting basic follow-ups.
Before this started causing trouble at work, were you already this forgetful as a kid or teenager?

Yeah, no, it was definitely there when I was a kid. I mean, I can remember grade school teachers saying I was smart — like, “she understands it when she pays attention,” that kind of thing — but I was always losing papers or leaving them in my desk, or missing part of the directions.

And they’d have to remind me to finish classwork. I’d start it, then somehow get off track, and then everyone else would be turning theirs in and I’d be like, wait, what are we doing? I used to think that was just me being messy, honestly. My backpack was a disaster too, but—sorry, that’s probably not the point. It was happening way before this job, yeah.
Outside of work, do you also have this same kind of trouble remembering and following through in your day-to-day life?

Yeah, I mean… outside work too, but honestly the work stuff is the biggest mess right now. Like the callbacks and work orders and all those little “I’ll get back to you” things — I say them like I’m going to remember, and then they just pile up.

At home it’s more like the same pattern, I guess, but work is where it’s really catching up to me because there are actual consequences. They sent me here because they’re worried I’m going to blow my chance to move up, which is… frustrating, because I really am trying.
Do you often find your mind drifting when someone is talking to you, even when you want to pay attention?

Yeah… yes, that happens a lot. Like my supervisor will be talking right to me about a repair or an audit thing, and I’m looking at him, nodding, trying to listen. But then only the first part really sticks, and by the time he’s on the next part I’m kind of… not gone exactly, but it’s not landing.

Then I have to ask him to repeat it, which is embarrassing because I was literally staring at him. And he’ll be like, “I just said that,” and I know he did, I just didn’t keep hold of it.
Do you often feel restless, like it’s hard to sit still?

Um… restless like physically? I don’t know if I’d call it that. I mean, I’m on my feet a lot at work anyway, so sitting still isn’t something I really think about much.

If I’m in a long meeting I might shift around or want it to be over, but honestly who doesn’t? I’m not sure that’s the same thing you mean. I don’t really have a clear answer on that one.
In conversations with family or friends, do you also lose track of what the other person is saying?

Yeah, I mean… with family or friends it can happen, but the clearest example is honestly at work. Like my supervisor will be talking straight to me about a repair or some audit thing, and I’m looking right at him, really trying to listen, and then only the first part sticks.

Then the rest kind of slips past me, and I end up having to ask him to say it again. It’s embarrassing because I’m not ignoring him, I’m right there. It just doesn’t stay put.
At home, do you also get distracted and lose track of what you’re doing?

Yeah, I mean… it’s not just conversations. Like, I’ll start a digital work order thinking, okay, I’ve got this, I’m reading the notes, and then halfway through my mind just kind of slips off.

Sometimes it’s because I hear a noise or I’m thinking about the next job I’m supposed to get to, and then I look back at the screen and realize I don’t actually know what I just read. So I have to start over, which is frustrating because I was right there doing it.
Do you spend a lot of time worrying, even when there isn’t an immediate problem to solve?

Um… worrying? I don’t know. I mean, I worry when there’s something happening, like if something at work is backed up or I forgot to pick up something from the store—actually I did that last week with laundry detergent, and then I had to stop after work and the traffic was ridiculous.

But, sorry, what were you asking—like worrying for no reason? I’m not sure. I don’t really think of myself as sitting around worrying all the time. I’d have to pay more attention to that, I guess.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

Um… down or depressed? I don’t know. I wouldn’t say depressed, I guess. I mean, I get frustrated, sure—like when the day gets away from me or I’m driving home and thinking about all the stuff I didn’t finish, and then I’ll remember I still have to deal with dinner or whatever.

But “down” like… every day, all the time? I’m not sure. I haven’t really been tracking it like that. What do you mean exactly by depressed?
In your home life, do these attention problems cause trouble for you too?

Yeah… at home too, but honestly the bigger mess has been work. I know you asked home life—sorry. It all kind of bleeds together.

Like, I come home and I’m thinking about the backlog I’ve got, and tenants have been complaining because things aren’t getting done fast enough. Then there was this safety review that ended up on my record, which… I keep thinking about that. I was working toward moving up, you know, and now I’m scared this is going to ruin that path.

So yeah, it causes trouble at home because I’m carrying it around with me, but the serious part right now is work.
At home, do you often forget everyday tasks like paying bills, appointments, or returning messages?

Yeah, I mean… at home, yes, but the thing that’s really gotten bad is callbacks and work orders. I’ll tell someone, “Yeah, I’ll follow up with you,” and then it just—unless it’s right in front of me, it disappears.

And then I’ll remember later, like while I’m making dinner or looking for my keys, and I think, okay, I need to call them back, but then something else happens and it’s gone again. It’s not even just messages, it’s scheduled callbacks, basic follow-ups I promised people… and now it’s piled up.

That’s kind of what brought me in, honestly. Work sent me here because it’s getting to the point where I’m scared I’m going to lose my chance at moving up.
At home, do you also leave chores or other everyday tasks unfinished because you get distracted?

Yeah… I mean, chores, sure, but it’s the same pattern I have at work, honestly. I’ll start something, and I’ll do the main part—like with a maintenance job, I’ll actually fix the thing. The sink works, the breaker’s dealt with, whatever.

But then the last steps just… somehow don’t happen. Like I won’t close out the ticket, or I’ll forget to label the panel, or I’m supposed to check back with the tenant and make sure it’s all okay, and I just move on because someone else is asking me something or I notice another problem.

And then later it looks like I didn’t finish the job, even though in my head I did the hard part already. That’s the part that gets me in trouble.
When you forget something, does it usually come back to you later once you get a reminder or see the situation again?

Yeah, sometimes it comes back when I see it again, like if the work order is sitting there or somebody calls again and I’m like, oh God, I was supposed to call you back.

But that’s kind of the problem—it comes back after it’s already piled up. What brought me in is I keep forgetting scheduled callbacks and work orders and even basic follow-ups I promised people. And then it’s not just one thing anymore, it’s a whole stack of them, and work sent me here because I’m scared I’m going to lose my shot at moving up.
When someone tells you something important, do you usually realize you missed parts of it right in the moment?

Yeah… I mean, sometimes I don’t realize it right away, which is embarrassing. Like my supervisor will be standing right there telling me about a repair or an audit thing, and I’m looking at him, nodding, trying to take it in.

But then only the first part really sticks. He’ll say three things and I’ll catch the first one, and then by the time he’s on the rest I’m sort of… I don’t know, I’m there but it’s not all landing. Then I have to ask him to repeat it, and I hate doing that because I feel like it looks like I wasn’t listening.
If you write things down right away or set phone reminders, do you usually remember to follow through?

I try to, yeah. Like I’ll write something on a scrap of paper or put it in my phone, and for a minute I feel like, okay, handled. But then… I don’t always actually follow through.

It’s the scheduled callbacks and work orders that are killing me right now. I’ll promise somebody I’ll get back to them, or there’s a follow-up I’m supposed to do, and then it slips until someone brings it up again. And now it’s piled up so bad that work sent me here, basically before I mess up my chance at moving up.

And I know that sounds dramatic, but it’s like—my phone has reminders, but if I’m in the middle of something or I swipe it away, then it’s gone. Then I’m off doing the next thing.
Do you often put off starting tasks, even when you know they’re important?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, I know there are things I don’t start right away, but I don’t always think of it as “putting it off.” Sometimes I’ll be about to start, and then something else comes up, or I go looking for one tool and notice some other thing that needs fixing, and then I’m halfway into that.

But, yeah… I don’t know. Important is tricky, because at work everything feels important when somebody’s standing there needing it done. I guess I’d have to think about it more.
Do you often lose or misplace things you need, like keys, tools, paperwork, or your phone?

Yeah, all the time. I mean, it sounds ridiculous, but I’ll have the tablet in my hand, set it down for one second, and then I’m walking around trying to figure out where I put it. Same with keys, flashlight, whatever tool I was just using.

And then it turns into this whole thing where the job is basically stopped because I’m hunting for something that should be right there. I know maintenance work is already like that sometimes—you’re up and down, in closets, mechanical rooms, people asking you questions—but it happens enough that people notice. It makes me look careless, and I hate that, because I’m not trying to be. It’s like the thing just disappears the second I’m not looking at it.
When you do pay full attention to something, do you usually remember it later?

If I’m fully locked in, I think I remember it better, yeah. But that’s kind of the problem — at work I’ll mean to remember something, like a callback or a work order or some follow-up I told someone I’d handle, and then the day keeps moving.

Like someone will stop me in the hall, then there’s a repair, then a tenant needs something, and I’m thinking, “Okay, I’ll call them back after this,” and then it’s just… gone. That’s really what brought me in. It’s piled up enough that work basically sent me here, because I don’t want to blow my chance at moving up over forgetting stuff I promised I’d do.
Before age 12, were these same attention and forgetfulness problems causing trouble both at school and at home?

Yeah, I think so. I remember being like that way back in grade school, before work or bills or any of this stuff. Teachers would say I was bright, but I was always losing papers or turning in something with parts missing because I didn’t catch all the directions.

At home it was kind of the same, like I’d need reminders to finish homework or whatever I was supposed to be doing. My mom would get frustrated because it wasn’t that I couldn’t do it, I just… didn’t finish unless someone kept bringing me back to it.

target_item.reason: The question is directly about what happens when she forgets tasks or follow-ups and whether reminders or seeing the situation again trigger her memory, which fits daily activities forgetfulness.

patient.answer:
Yeah, sometimes it comes back when I see it again, like if the work order is sitting there or somebody calls again and I’m like, oh God, I was supposed to call you back.

But that’s kind of the problem—it comes back after it’s already piled up. What brought me in is I keep forgetting scheduled callbacks and work orders and even basic follow-ups I promised people. And then it’s not just one thing anymore, it’s a whole stack of them, and work sent me here because I’m scared I’m going to lose my shot at moving up.

doctor.intent: Differentiate lifelong inattentive ADHD from a primary memory disorder by testing whether the problem is mainly failure to encode information because attention drifts.
doctor.question: When someone tells you something important, do you usually realize you missed parts of it right in the moment?

target_item.name: Listening_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: When my supervisor talks straight to me about a repair or audit, I’ll be looking right at him, but only the first part sticks and then I have to ask him to say it again.
target_item.reason: The question is about missing parts of important information when someone is speaking directly to me, which matches listening difficulty.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, sometimes I don’t realize it right away, which is embarrassing. Like my supervisor will be standing right there telling me about a repair or an audit thing, and I’m looking at him, nodding, trying to take it in.

But then only the first part really sticks. He’ll say three things and I’ll catch the first one, and then by the time he’s on the rest I’m sort of… I don’t know, I’m there but it’s not all landing. Then I have to ask him to repeat it, and I hate doing that because I feel like it looks like I wasn’t listening.

doctor.intent: Differentiate lifelong ADHD-related inattention from a primary memory disorder by checking whether recall improves with external organization.
doctor.question: If you write things down right away or set phone reminders, do you usually remember to follow through?

target_item.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
target_item.manifestation: What brought me in is I keep forgetting scheduled callbacks, work orders, and even basic follow-ups I promised people, and now it’s piled up so much that work sent me here before I lose my shot at moving up.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether reminders or writing things down help with remembering callbacks, follow-ups, and other daily responsibilities, which directly matches forgetfulness in daily activities.

patient.answer:
I try to, yeah. Like I’ll write something on a scrap of paper or put it in my phone, and for a minute I feel like, okay, handled. But then… I don’t always actually follow through.

It’s the scheduled callbacks and work orders that are killing me right now. I’ll promise somebody I’ll get back to them, or there’s a follow-up I’m supposed to do, and then it slips until someone brings it up again. And now it’s piled up so bad that work sent me here, basically before I mess up my chance at moving up.

And I know that sounds dramatic, but it’s like—my phone has reminders, but if I’m in the middle of something or I swipe it away, then it’s gone. Then I’m off doing the next thing.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the core problem is task initiation/procrastination versus forgetting after starting, which helps distinguish ADHD-related executive dysfunction from a primary memory disorder.
doctor.question: Do you often put off starting tasks, even when you know they’re important?

target_item.reason: The question is about procrastinating or delaying the start of important tasks, which is not directly covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, I know there are things I don’t start right away, but I don’t always think of it as “putting it off.” Sometimes I’ll be about to start, and then something else comes up, or I go looking for one tool and notice some other thing that needs fixing, and then I’m halfway into that.

But, yeah… I don’t know. Important is tricky, because at work everything feels important when somebody’s standing there needing it done. I guess I’d have to think about it more.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms reflect ADHD-related disorganization by assessing frequent loss or misplacement of necessary items.
doctor.question: Do you often lose or misplace things you need, like keys, tools, paperwork, or your phone?

target_item.name: Losing_Items
target_item.manifestation: I’m constantly hunting for the tablet, keys, flashlight, or the one tool I had in my hand a minute ago, and it’s gotten bad enough that it holds up jobs and makes me look careless.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about frequently losing or misplacing necessary items like keys, tools, paperwork, or phone.

patient.answer:
Yeah, all the time. I mean, it sounds ridiculous, but I’ll have the tablet in my hand, set it down for one second, and then I’m walking around trying to figure out where I put it. Same with keys, flashlight, whatever tool I was just using.

And then it turns into this whole thing where the job is basically stopped because I’m hunting for something that should be right there. I know maintenance work is already like that sometimes—you’re up and down, in closets, mechanical rooms, people asking you questions—but it happens enough that people notice. It makes me look careless, and I hate that, because I’m not trying to be. It’s like the thing just disappears the second I’m not looking at it.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there is a true memory-storage problem versus information not being encoded because of inattention, to distinguish ADHD from a primary memory disorder.
doctor.question: When you do pay full attention to something, do you usually remember it later?

target_item.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
target_item.manifestation: What brought me in is I keep forgetting scheduled callbacks, work orders, and even basic follow-ups I promised people, and now it’s piled up so much that work sent me here before I lose my shot at moving up.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about remembering things later, which most directly relates to the forgetfulness in daily activities described in this profile.

patient.answer:
If I’m fully locked in, I think I remember it better, yeah. But that’s kind of the problem — at work I’ll mean to remember something, like a callback or a work order or some follow-up I told someone I’d handle, and then the day keeps moving.

Like someone will stop me in the hall, then there’s a repair, then a tenant needs something, and I’m thinking, “Okay, I’ll call them back after this,” and then it’s just… gone. That’s really what brought me in. It’s piled up enough that work basically sent me here, because I don’t want to blow my chance at moving up over forgetting stuff I promised I’d do.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the attention problems reflect longstanding ADHD impairment across multiple settings rather than memory loss, anxiety, depression, or stress-related symptoms.
doctor.question: Before age 12, were these same attention and forgetfulness problems causing trouble both at school and at home?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I remember being this way back in grade school, long before any of this job pressure—teachers said I was bright but always misplaced papers, missed parts of directions, and needed reminders to finish classwork.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the attention and forgetfulness problems were present and impairing before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I think so. I remember being like that way back in grade school, before work or bills or any of this stuff. Teachers would say I was bright, but I was always losing papers or turning in something with parts missing because I didn’t catch all the directions.

At home it was kind of the same, like I’d need reminders to finish homework or whatever I was supposed to be doing. My mom would get frustrated because it wasn’t that I couldn’t do it, I just… didn’t finish unless someone kept bringing me back to it.

inference.note: Childhood-onset and persistent cross-situational inattention/forgetfulness are now clearly established (school, home, work), with distractibility, losing things, failing to finish tasks/follow-through, and no convincing evidence for primary anxiety, depressive, trauma-related, or memory disorder; presentation narrows to ADHD predominantly inattentive type.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: History is most consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation: longstanding inattentive symptoms beginning in childhood, present across school/home/work settings, and currently causing clear occupational impairment. Hyperactive/impulsive symptoms were not clearly endorsed, supporting the inattentive subtype. Anxiety and depression were not substantiated as primary explanations.
